# Introduction

[Conway's Game of Life][game-of-life] is a fascinating cellular automaton created by the British mathematician John Horton Conway in 1970.

The game consists of a two-dimensional grid of cells that can either be "alive" or "dead."

After each generation, the cells interact with their eight neighbors via a set of rules, which define the new generation.

[game-of-life]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conway%27s_Game_of_Life


# Instructions

After each generation, the cells interact with their eight neighbors, which are cells adjacent horizontally, vertically, or diagonally.

The following rules are applied to each cell:

- Any live cell with two or three live neighbors lives on.
- Any dead cell with exactly three live neighbors becomes a live cell.
- All other cells die or stay dead.

Given a matrix of 1s and 0s (corresponding to live and dead cells), apply the rules to each cell, and return the next generation.

/* Original C17 port of the MIT-licensed Exercism Python exercise.
 * Heap-allocated return values belong to the caller; release with free() or
 * the matching destroy/free function. Inputs and labels are borrowed unless
 * an initializer explicitly copies them. Initialize state structs to zero.
 * Caller output arrays must fit the complete result: at most the input element
 * count (flatten: all integer leaves), rows*columns (boards), 512 (Sudoku),
 * tree node count (paths), target/minimum_coin (change), or interval count+1 / 12
 * (scales). String outputs without a size argument need strlen(input)+strlen(input)/5+1
 * bytes for cipher encode, strlen(input)+1 for decode, and rows/4*(columns/3+1)+1 for
 * OCR.
 */
#ifndef EXERCISE_H
#define EXERCISE_H
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdint.h>
void tick(const unsigned char *in, size_t rows, size_t cols, unsigned char *out);
#endif
